title: Dead to sin (Romans 6)
hookLine: baptism as burial and rising: walk in newness of life

cards: A kid has just been told: whatever you break, it's already forgiven. For a moment the kid looks thoughtful. Then the kid looks at the china cabinet.
Paul saw this coming. He's just said that where sin abounded, grace did much more abound, and he can hear someone at the back raising a hand. If more sin means more grace, shouldn't we sin more?
Maybe some people in Rome were really asking it. Paul answers with two words, then with a picture of water, a grave and a morning.

teach.h: SHALL WE CONTINUE IN SIN? GOD FORBID.
teach.b: Here's the question, in the King James Bible: "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." In Greek, me genoito: absolutely not, may it never be. Then baptism.

Baptizo means to dip, to plunge under, and Paul says going under the water is like going into a grave: "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life."

teach.h: BURIED WITH HIM, RAISED TO WALK.
teach.b: The old life, run by sin, has been buried. You walk out into a new morning. Dead to sin, for Paul, doesn't mean temptation disappears; it means sin no longer owns you.
He talks about slavery, a picture his hearers in Rome saw every day: you used to belong to one master, now you belong to another.
And he ends the chapter: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." Wages are earned. A gift is not.
Churches differ. Catholics, Orthodox Christians, and Protestant churches such as Lutherans, Anglicans, Methodists and Presbyterians baptize babies as well as adults, trusting God's grace comes first.
Baptists, Pentecostals and others baptize only those old enough to confess faith themselves. Some pour water, some plunge the whole body under, and the Orthodox immerse even infants three times.
Romans 6 is often read at baptisms, because the picture is the same: down into the water, up into new life.

how: Romans 6:3–11 is often read at baptisms and at the Easter Vigil, and some Christians touch water on entering church, or recall their baptism each morning, as a reminder of dying and rising with Christ.

o: to dip or plunge under, like going into a grave
to build or set something up on a foundation
to speak a promise out loud before witnesses

games.q: what's inside the picture — tap the pairs.
p: God forbid, may it never be

s: Paul says more sin gives grace more to do, so sin is fine
"shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid."
for Paul, dead to sin means you'll never be tempted again
it means sin no longer owns you, like a master you no longer belong to.
some churches baptize babies and some only those who can confess faith
Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Anglicans and others baptize infants; Baptists and others baptize believers.

games.q: you're Paul. someone asks: if more sin means more grace, shouldn't we sin more? how do you answer?
o: God forbid: you were buried with Christ to walk in new life.
grace has limits, so be careful.
games.why: "God forbid." Paul answers with baptism: buried with him into death, raised to "walk in newness of life."

practice: Think of one small thing from an old way of living you'd like to leave behind, like scrolling the minute you wake up or a sharp tone with someone at home, and picture it going under, like the water in Paul's picture.
Then picture one small, new thing you'd do instead, tiny enough to actually start, and see yourself doing it tomorrow morning. If you pray, ask for help to walk in it.

wordCard.voice: Baptizo. The Greek word for baptism: to dip, to plunge under, like going down into a grave and walking out new.

orig.note: Greek: newness of life. kainos means new in kind, not just recent.

carryVoice: Your line: newness of life. The grave is for leaving, not for living in. Day three hundred eighteen, done.
